relevance_reason: Reports three new families with HDBSCC, three novel homozygous JAM3 mutations, and functional studies of their effect on the protein.

findings.statement: Akawi et al. (2013) described a Turkish girl whose parents were second cousins. She was born at term weighing 2480 g (below the 10th centile). On day 5 she was admitted with tonic seizures that did not respond to treatment. Examination showed a 30-cm head circumference, a sloping forehead, a bulging anterior fontanel, bitemporal grooving, and bilateral nuclear cataracts. Brain CT showed subependymal calcification and multifocal intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Infection serologies and platelet levels were normal. She developed posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus and died at 2 months of age; an older preterm sister had intracranial bleeding and died in the neonatal period.
quotes: The parents of the affected child in this family are second cousins of Turkish origin.
Physical examination revealed a head circumference of 30 cm, slopping forehead, prominent, bulging anterior fontanelle, bitemporal grooving and bilateral nuclear cataracts (Figure 2A-1).
Brain computerized tomography showed calcification of the subependymal region and multifocal intraparenchymal hemorrhage (Figure 2A-2).

findings.statement: Akawi et al. (2013) described 2 affected brothers born to healthy, nonconsanguineous parents of Afghani origin. The first had bilateral cataracts and feeding problems from birth. At 2 weeks he presented with vomiting, irritability, and a high-pitched cry. MRI at 15 days showed grade IV intraventricular hemorrhage, severe ventricular dilatation, white matter abnormalities, and multiple subependymal cysts, and renal ultrasound showed horseshoe kidneys. Extensive metabolic, genetic, and coagulation investigations were normal, and he died at 2 weeks. The second brother had bilateral cataracts at birth. He deteriorated on day 5 with a fall in hemoglobin, bilateral epileptiform activity on EEG, and extensive bilateral intracerebral hemorrhage, and died on the fifth day of life; he also had pelvicalyceal dilatation of the right kidney.
quotes: Brain MRI at the age of 15 days showed Grade IV intraventricular haemorrhage, severe ventricular dilatation and white matter abnormalities in both cerebral hemispheres and multiple subependymal cysts (Figure 2B).
Renal ultrasound showed horseshoe kidneys with echogenic cortex and altered corticomedullary differentiation.
Cranial ultrasound revealed extensive bilateral intracerebral haemorrhage. He died on the fifth day of life. Abdominal ultrasound showed pelvicalyceal dilatation of the right kidney.

findings.statement: Akawi et al. (2013) described a girl whose parents were Moroccan first cousins. She had central and nuclear bilateral cataracts at birth. On day 2 she presented with irritability and a bulging fontanel. CT and MRI showed multifocal intraparenchymal and intraventricular hemorrhages, subependymal calcification, diffuse brain edema, cystic changes, dilated ventricles, and a thin corpus callosum. EEG showed electrical status epilepticus without clinical seizures, and she had severe anemia. Her head circumference reached 41 cm (+4 SD), and she died at 39 days. One sib died at 10 days with cerebral hemorrhage and hydrocephalus, and another was stillborn with hydrocephalus and necrotic cerebral tissue.
quotes: The parents are first cousins of Moroccan origin, who had a total of five pregnancies.
Head CT revealed multifocal intraparenchymal hemorrhages, subependymal calcification and diffusely hypodense brain parenchyma (Figure 2C-2).

MRI of the brain revealed intraventricular and intraparenchymal hemorrhage, edema and cystic changes of the brain parenchyma, dilated ventricles and thin corpus callosum with haemohrragic damage (Figure 2C-3).

findings.statement: Akawi et al. (2013) summarized the shared phenotype across these families. All affected children had bilateral cataracts and progressive neurologic impairment, with seizures in some. Neuroimaging in all patients showed intraparenchymal hemorrhage with brain destruction and subependymal, basal ganglia, and white matter calcification. Renal anomalies and liver enlargement were more variable. Counting the original family, the disorder was lethal in 7 of 10 cases within the first weeks of life, and the 3 survivors were severely retarded with severe spasticity and seizures.
quotes: All the affected children in this report had bilateral cataracts and develop progressive neurological impairment, associated with seizures in some individuals.
In addition neuro-imaging in all patients showed intraparanchymal hemorrhage with evidence of brain destruction and subependymal, basal ganglia and white matter calcification.
The disorder was lethal in 7 out of the 10 cases. Death occurred in the first few weeks of life. Those who survived (3 in total) are severely retarded with severe spasticity and seizures.

findings.statement: In the affected Turkish girl from family 1, Akawi et al. (2013) found a homozygous c.656G>A transition in exon 6 of the JAM3 gene by sequencing, resulting in a cys219-to-tyr (C219Y) substitution in the Ig-like C2-type domain. The mutation segregated with the disorder, was absent from dbSNP and the 1000 Genomes Project, and affected a conserved residue. In transfected HeLa cells, the C219Y mutant was retained mostly in the endoplasmic reticulum rather than reaching the plasma membrane. The authors suggested that loss of a disulfide bond causes misfolding and a trafficking defect.
quotes: In family 1 we detected a non-synonomous mutation (c.656G>A) in exon 6 of JAM3 gene, which led to an amino acid substitution at position 219 (p.C219Y).
the p.C219Y mutant co-localized predominantly with the ER marker (calnexin) and not with GFP-hRas indicating its retention in the ER (Figure 3 panels M–R, Supp. Figure S2).

findings.statement: In the 2 affected Afghani brothers from family 2, Akawi et al. (2013) found a homozygous c.346G>A transition in exon 4 of JAM3, resulting in a glu116-to-lys (E116K) substitution in the Ig-like V-type domain. The mutation segregated with the disorder and was absent from dbSNP and the 1000 Genomes Project. The E116K mutant reached the plasma membrane normally in HeLa cells. The authors suggested that it may disrupt dimerization or interaction with partner proteins.
quotes: In family 2 we identified a single nucleotide substituation (c.346G>A) in exon 4 of JAM3 leading to a missense mutation at position 116 (p.E116K).
The p.E116K mutant traffics normally to the plasma membrane as the wild-type and may have lost its function due to the lack of interaction with an interacting partner.

findings.statement: In the Moroccan family (family 3), Akawi et al. (2013) found a homozygous c.2T>G transversion in JAM3 that changes the initiator methionine to arginine (M1R). The mutation segregated with the disorder and was absent from dbSNP and the 1000 Genomes Project. The authors predicted that it impairs protein synthesis.
quotes: The third mutation (c.2T>G) changed the initiator codon (methionine) of JAM3 leading to amino acid substitution to arginine (p.M1R).
The p.M1R mutation affects the start codon and therefore is predicted to impair protein synthesis.

findings.statement: Akawi et al. (2013) found that in all 3 families the mutations segregated with the disorder in a pattern consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. Parents were heterozygous carriers, and unaffected sibs were either homozygous wildtype or heterozygous.
quotes: Furthermore, the detected mutations segregated with disease status in the three families; the parents were heterozygous, consistent with carrier status and the available unaffected siblings were homozygous for the wild type or heterozygous for the mutation.

findings.statement: Akawi et al. (2013) noted that the missense mutations affected different domains of JAM3, yet the affected children had similar phenotypes. They suggested this clinical homogeneity is likely due to total loss of protein function.
quotes: Our study revealed several missense mutations scattered throughout the coding sequence of JAM3 affecting different domains yet the affected children shared similar phenotype indicating homogeneity of this disorder at the clinical and molecular level. This is likely due to total loss of the protein function as a result of those mutations.

relevance_reason: This is the original report defining HDBSCC. It describes a consanguineous family, maps the locus to 11q25 and identifies a homozygous JAM3 splice-site mutation.

findings.statement: Mochida et al. (2010) described members of a large consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates who had a rare autosomal recessive syndrome. Its features were severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts. The presentation overlapped with some reported cases of pseudo-TORCH syndrome and with patients who have occludin mutations, but massive intracranial hemorrhage set these patients apart.
quotes: Some members of this family had a rare autosomal-recessive syndrome characterized by severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts.

Their clinical presentation overlaps with some reported cases of pseudo-TORCH syndrome as well as with cases involving mutations in occludin, another component of the tight-junction complex. However, massive intracranial hemorrhage distinguishes these patients from others.

findings.statement: Mochida et al. (2010) used homozygosity mapping in the consanguineous UAE family to map the disease locus to chromosome 11q25. The maximum multipoint lod score was 6.15.
quotes: Homozygosity mapping identified the disease locus in this family on chromosome 11q25 with a maximum multipoint LOD score of 6.15.

findings.statement: Mochida et al. (2010) sequenced genes in the 11q25 candidate interval and found a homozygous mutation in the JAM3 gene in affected members of the consanguineous UAE family. The mutation affects the canonical splice-donor site of intron 5. RT-PCR analysis of a patient lymphoblast cell line confirmed abnormal splicing, which leads to a frameshift with early termination.
quotes: Sequence analysis of genes in the candidate interval uncovered a mutation in the canonical splice-donor site of intron 5 of JAM3.
RT-PCR analysis of a patient lymphoblast cell line confirmed abnormal splicing, leading to a frameshift mutation with early termination.
we identified a homozygous mutation in the tight-junction protein gene JAM3 in a large consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates

variants.as_reported: mutation in the canonical splice-donor site of intron 5 of JAM3

findings.statement: Mochida et al. (2010) noted that JAM3, a tight-junction protein, is known to be present in vascular endothelium. They suggested that JAM3 is essential for maintaining the integrity of the cerebrovascular endothelium and for normal lens development in humans.
quotes: JAM3 is known to be present in vascular endothelium, although its roles in cerebral vasculature have not been implicated.
Our results suggest that JAM3 is essential for maintaining the integrity of the cerebrovascular endothelium as well as for normal lens development in humans.
